You don't need the $100 Gemini plan anymore.

Since yesterday the $20 one has Gemini 4 Neon. In an independent test on 105 bugs planted in real code, it beat GPT-6.2 Astra and Fable 5.2.

The scoreboard (Paweł Huryn, 2 repos, find and fix what you can):
→ Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh): 63
→ GPT-6.2 Astra (max): 62.7
→ Fable 5.2 (max): 58
→ Gemini 4 Carbon (high): 57.3

Carbon is the model you were paying $100 for. Neon is in Google AI Pro at $19.99, and in the API at $3 in and $15 out per million tokens.

One honest caveat: that's one test at his effort settings. The app may run Neon lower. So don't switch on a scoreboard. Switch on your own work.

3 prompts to decide in one evening:

Prompt 1: Same task, two models
"Here is a real task from my week: [paste]. Solve it. Then list every assumption you made, every spot you're unsure about, and what you'd check before shipping. Score your answer 1 to 10 against this done line: [what finished looks like]."
Run it in Neon and in the model you pay for now. The lower self-score that's still right wins.

Prompt 2: Bring your setup with you
"I'm testing a new AI model. Here are my custom instructions from my current one and the 3 prompts I use most: [paste]. The new model knows nothing about me or my past chats. Rewrite each one so it works cold: add who I am, what I'm working on, what good output looks like and the format I want. Flag anything that only worked because my old model remembered me."

Prompt 3: Your routing rule
"Here are the 5 tasks I ran in both models and how each did: [task, model, score, what went wrong]. Sort them into three groups: Neon wins, my current model wins, too close to call. Then write a one-paragraph rule for which model gets which kind of task, and tell me if I can drop a subscription."

If you're on the $100 plan and Neon wins most of your tasks, that's $80 a month back. If it doesn't, you'll know exactly what you're paying for.

You paste contracts, client lists and passwords into AI tools every day.

A security team just planted 2 million fake secrets in AI services to see where they'd end up. Some got stolen and used. One link showed up in a stranger's chat 24 days later.

What they found (HD Moore's team at Dragos, July to November):
→ 3 AI hosting companies got breached. A couple hundred planted cloud keys were stolen and used for tens of thousands of calls
→ Resellers on an AI marketplace kept people's prompts through plain request logs. No hack needed
→ One lab opened secret links from more than half the prompts sent to it, including about 2 in 3 marked "don't store"
→ Of about 2,000 routes traced, several hundred passed through systems nobody could identify

The worst of it sat in the middle: the $5 app, the reseller, the router you never picked. The researchers' own advice is to go direct to a major provider, or not paste it at all.

3 steps for the stuff you can't stop pasting:

Prompt 1: Scrub before you paste
"Clean this text before I share it with any AI tool. Replace every person's name, company, email, phone number, address, account number, password, API key, link and money amount with a placeholder like [CLIENT_1] or [AMOUNT_2]. Keep the meaning and structure. Give me the cleaned text, then a separate key table so I can swap the real values back."
Run it only in the main app you pay for directly. Everything else gets the clean copy.

Prompt 2: Audit my AI stack
"Here's every AI tool I use for work: [apps, browser extensions, bots, plugins, anywhere I pasted an API key]. For each one, tell me who runs the model behind it, whether my text passes through another company on the way, and what their policy says about storing or training on my data. If you don't know, write 'unknown' and tell me exactly where to check. End with three lists: keep, check this week, stop pasting work into."

Step 3: Plant your own canary
Get a free tracking link at http://canarytokens.org, put it in a fake "passwords" note, and paste that into the tool you trust least. If anyone ever opens it, you get an email.

The safest secret is the one you never pasted.
